action: Update WordPress to 7.1.5 now (Dashboard, Updates), or confirm the background auto-update ran; older branches are being backported, so watch for those releases.
exec: WordPress runs a large share of company websites, and this release fixes an unauthenticated flaw the project says could lead to remote code execution.
plain: WordPress released an update fixing about 20 security problems, including one that lets someone without an account gain higher access and possibly run code. Site owners should update now.

key_findings: Unauthenticated privilege escalation via Template Part block attributes that the post says could lead to remote code execution.
Multisite: a site Administrator can take over a Super Admin account via Customizer menu previews.
Two SQL injection fixes (WP_Meta_Query and Customizer changeset front-page setting) and unauthenticated stored XSS via comment shortcode attributes.
The post does not mention exploitation in the wild.
recommendations: Update immediately; automatic background updates begin on sites that support them.

summary: WordPress 7.1.5, released November 18, is a security release listing 20 items, including unauthenticated privilege escalation through Template Part block attributes that the project says could lead to remote code execution. It also fixes two SQL injections, a Multisite Super Admin takeover and stored XSS in comments. The project recommends updating immediately and does not report exploitation.
title: WordPress 7.1.5 security release fixes unauthenticated privilege escalation and SQL injection

validation.note: WordPress.org release post and GBHackers agree on release date, the Template Part flaw, SQL injection and XSS fixes. Neither gives CVE ids. Patchstack (18 Nov) also lists the fixes, states no CVE ids had been assigned at publication and does not report exploitation.

review.note: Compared title, 18 Nov date, 20 items, Template Part unauthenticated privilege escalation/RCE wording, two SQLi, Multisite Super Admin, comment XSS, no exploitation stated, update advice against WordPress.org post and GBHackers
